Getting started — five minutes to a streaming 3D scene#

Verse Engine turns a GLB into a URL that streams in the browser — a 283 MB apartment shows its first picture in about 4 seconds over the internet, and a 30-million-triangle scan runs at over 100 fps on a laptop, because the viewer fetches a coarse version first and then only the detail the camera can see. This page is the shortest path from a file on your disk to a scene on your own site. Every step works on the dev server (node web/playground/serve.mjs, port 8080) and on the production deployment identically; HOST below stands for either.

1. Upload a model (≈ 1 minute)#

Open the app at https://HOST/app and drop a file or choose one — a .glb is the quickest (everything you can upload). The file is checked in your browser before anything is uploaded, and you confirm two things before you press Publish:

  1. What is this? — what the check found (a product, a scan, an interior, a building…) and how it will be shown: Fidelity for a textured product or scan up to about 6 m (published as itself, live in about a second — Fidelity mode), Streamed for interiors, buildings, BIM, point clouds and splats. You can correct either.
  2. How should it look? — a studio look and background for a Fidelity product, or the Lighting choice for a live-lit streamed scene: Keep as exported (the default) or Bake for me (preview or final — Bake for me).

Among the advanced options there are two ways to open a file:

OptionWhenWhat happens
Automatic (recommended)anything, up to 512 MB (20 GB when prepared by a plug-in)a Fidelity product is published as itself in about a second; anything else the server builds into a streamed scene (a minute or two for products, about twenty minutes for a large building). You watch its progress with a countdown, then walk the scene and get a link
This device onlysmall textured productsthe GLB opens whole in your browser with full PBR textures; nothing is uploaded and no link is created

If a build struggles it is retried on lighter settings by itself. A model (up to 96 MB) that still cannot be streamed is published in compatibility mode: the link works at full quality, as one larger download.

Draco-compressed, KHR-quantized and WebP/KTX2-textured files are accepted and normalized server-side. Gaussian-splat captures (.splat or 3DGS .ply) upload the same way as models: small ones load instantly in the browser, larger ones compile into a streamed .vsp and hand back a share link just like a GLB (browsers with WebGPU only; add X-Verse-Kind: splat when using the API directly).

Prefer the API? The same thing from a shell:

Code
curl -X POST https://HOST/v1/ingest \
  -H "Content-Type: model/gltf-binary" -H "X-Verse-Name: chair" \
  --data-binary @chair.glb
# → {"job":"chair-9f3a01b2c4d5"}
curl https://HOST/v1/ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5
# → {"status":"done","url":"https://HOST/?vpk=ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5.vpk", …}

Full protocol, keys and quotas: Ingest API.

2. Get a share link (≈ 10 seconds)#

When the build finishes, the scene opens with its link; Share copies it:

Code
https://HOST/app?vpk=ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5.vpk

Copy it. Anyone who opens it streams the scene — no account, no install — in a current browser, on a desktop or a phone (Browser support). The ingest/<id>.vpk part is the scene id you will use everywhere else. The file is Ed25519-signed by the server; browsers verify it and the viewer's status reads "Streaming · verified".

Scenes that get an automatic walkthrough also offer Tour and Export video — a client-ready MP4/WebM flythrough of the tour, recorded and downloaded entirely in your browser (pick duration and 1080p/720p/native; nothing is uploaded).

Review workflow. Every share link doubles as a review round: the viewer offers Review once the scene is up. Your client toggles it on, clicks any spot in the scene (orbit or walk mode alike), and types a note — the comment is pinned to that exact 3D position, no account needed. When you open the same link, the numbered pins show where every note lives; sign in as the scene's owner (with your email or WhatsApp code, or a Studio token) and each pin grows Resolve and Delete — resolved pins grey out and hide behind a "show resolved" toggle. Your Studio scene cards list open/resolved counts per scene. Comments cap at 500 characters and 200 per scene; on a private scene they are visible only with the share token or your own sign-in.

Want the link to open for your client only? Sign in, flip the scene to private and mint a per-recipient share token — Share privately with tokens.

Useful URL options in the app: ?model=<glb> (classic load), ?vpk=<url> (stream), ?experience=<manifest> (see step 4), ?inspector=1 (devtools panel), ?tier=c (force the WebGL2 fallback). Look and performance knobs (?ssr, ?hdr, ?exposure, ?env, ?post, ?render=demand, …) are in Tune quality knobs.

3. Embed it with one script tag (≈ 1 minute)#

Paste this into any HTML page — a CMS block, a product page, a Notion-style embed. The host page needs no header changes: the engine runs in an iframe served from the Verse origin, which carries the cross-origin-isolation headers it needs.

Code
<script src="https://HOST/embed.js" data-scene="chair-9f3a01b2c4d5"></script>

That is the whole integration. data-scene="<id>" resolves to ingest/<id>.vpk; data-vpk="<url>" and data-model="<glb>" are also accepted, and data-poster="poster.jpg" shows an image until the engine arrives (and if it never does — ad-blockers, offline — the poster stays).

Programmatic mount, when you want events and control:

Code
<div id="viewer"></div>
<script src="https://HOST/embed.js"></script>
<script>
  const viewer = Verse.embed(document.getElementById("viewer"), {
    scene: "chair-9f3a01b2c4d5",
  });
  viewer.on("ready",  (d) => console.log("tier", d.tier, "first frame in", d.ttfi, "ms"));
  viewer.on("loaded", (d) => console.log(d.clusters, "clusters"));
  viewer.on("dwell",  (d) => analytics.track("3d-dwell", d.ms));
  const hit = await viewer.pick(0.5, 0.5); // what is under the centre pixel?
</script>

Every verb and event — walk(), pick(), play(), spawnProp(), setDepthOfField(), goTo(), dwell, interact, signed, … — is in the Embed SDK reference. The typed contract ships as verse-embed.d.ts.

Degradation is automatic and telemetered: browsers with WebGPU get the full picture; browsers with only WebGL2 (older iPhones, many in-app browsers) get a lighter build; anything else gets the poster and a link to open the scene in a browser. The WebGL2 build streams the same scenes, with the same studio lighting, shadows, bloom and reflection probes (screen-space and ray-traced reflections, path-traced stills and splats stay WebGPU-only). See Browser support.

4. Compose an experience (≈ 2 minutes)#

A walkthrough is more than one mesh. An experience manifest is a JSON file on the Verse origin that places extra GLBs into a base scene, sets the lighting and ambience, and names the hotspots a visitor jumps between:

Code
{
  "name": "Showroom",
  "scene": "ingest/chair-9f3a01b2c4d5.vpk",
  "props": [{ "url": "props/lamp.glb", "position": [1.2, 0, -0.6], "yaw": 30 }],
  "ambience": { "particles": "dust@0,1.5,0*1", "audio": "wind@0,2,0" },
  "spawn": { "position": [0, 1.6, 3], "yaw": 180 },
  "hotspots": [
    { "id": "front", "label": "Front", "position": [0, 1.2, 3], "look": [0, 0.5, 0] },
    { "id": "side",  "label": "Side",  "position": [3, 1.2, 0], "look": [0, 0.5, 0] }
  ]
}

Save it as showroom.verse.json next to your assets and open

Code
https://HOST/?experience=showroom.verse.json

The app shows a button per hotspot. In an embed, viewer.load("showroom.verse.json") does the same and viewer.goTo("side") jumps; the experience event hands you the hotspot list to build your own UI. Every key is documented in Experience manifests.

Prefer not to hand-write JSON? Open your scene with &edit=1 and the experience editor authors the manifest live: capture the spawn and hotspots from where you stand, tap surfaces to place props and ambience, add more streamed scenes at offsets (the Scenes section — an apartment plus its clubhouse in one link), record a camera tour (⏺, replayed by ?tour= or viewer.load("….tour.json") in an embed), and grab a share poster (📸) for the embed's data-poster. Download the JSON or Publish for an instant share link.
